segments.title: British surveillance tracks any move by Graf Spee
segments.summary: Harwood's cruisers and a network of observers ashore make any departure by Admiral Graf Spee from Montevideo difficult to conceal.
segments.body: Commodore Harwood covers the approaches to Montevideo with three cruisers, which makes every departure route dangerous for Admiral Graf Spee. A move toward Argentina or a battle near Uruguay's three-mile territorial limit would create different problems. Merchant ships in the harbor can radio updates for a fine of only £5, which Britain would likely repay and might supplement with a reward. Ambassador Millington-Drake, MI6 officers, and the naval attache add official observers ashore. Harwood might also have an aircraft aloft once Graf Spee moves. This network makes even a night departure difficult to hide.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Harwood's cruiser coverage and the British observation and radio network around Graf Spee.

segments.title: Langsdorff prepares for Uruguay's deadline
segments.summary: With the 72-hour limit expiring the next day, Langsdorff refuses to surrender or sacrifice his crew and starts moving people and stores for the plan he has chosen.
segments.body: Langsdorff's options narrow as Graf Spee's permitted stay approaches its end. He will neither surrender nor sacrifice roughly a thousand sailors in a hopeless action, because he believes a thousand living heroes are better than a thousand dead ones. He continues to seek more time while preparing on the assumption that Uruguay will refuse it. A German vessel sits between Graf Spee and the shore as cover, while German-owned tugs from Argentina move closer and begin transferring people and stores. Those preparations show that his plan for the next day is already under way.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses the 72-hour deadline, Langsdorff's refusal to sacrifice his crew, and preparations involving German vessels and tugs.

segments.title: Four frantic days cannot restore Graf Spee
segments.summary: The Montevideo episode compresses a long South Atlantic campaign into four days of intense activity that cannot restore Graf Spee to fighting condition.
segments.body: The wider South Atlantic campaign contains long stretches of sailing and waiting, followed by the sudden tempo of the Battle of the River Plate and the Montevideo crisis. Graf Spee spends three days in port, and the fourth will bring the episode to its conclusion. Repairs restore part of the ship's capability, but never enough for her to fight her way out. Diplomatic and logistical work continues at speed even though it cannot change the basic military position. A slow commerce-raiding campaign has become a crisis governed by port deadlines and approaching enemy forces.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the wider campaign's slow periods with four frantic days and says Graf Spee cannot be repaired enough to fight out.

segments.title: Battle damage compounds Graf Spee's machinery wear
segments.summary: Reports of engine trouble suggest that combat may have worsened machinery wear caused by prolonged operations without servicing.
segments.body: Some reports attribute Graf Spee's engine and piston problems to battle damage, while others suggest that long service without maintenance caused at least part of the trouble. The evidence in this account does not settle the issue. Royal Navy reports on heavily used ships offer a broader comparison: machinery worn by long operations often develops worse problems after combat. That possibility matters when judging why Graf Spee could not regain full fighting condition in Montevideo. Operational endurance also depends on whether a ship has had time to service its machinery.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses engine and piston reports, extended use without servicing, and battle worsening existing machinery wear.

segments.title: British cruisers refuel as reinforcements close
segments.summary: Ajax and Achilles refuel, Cumberland carries the stronger ammunition reserve, and Renown and Ark Royal hurry toward the River Plate.
segments.body: Ajax and Achilles refuel from a Royal Fleet Auxiliary vessel, while Cumberland still has ample fuel and more ammunition. The replenishment keeps Harwood's cruiser force ready if Graf Spee sails before heavier reinforcements arrive. Renown and Ark Royal approach at full speed and expect to stop in Brazil on the way. Ark Royal is making more than 30 knots, and some of her engineers later claimed that this was the fastest she ever sailed. Her captain's demand for every possible knot captures the urgency of the approach. Fuel, ammunition, machinery effort, and arrival time all shape Britain's plan for Graf Spee's possible departure.

evidence.note: The transcript describes fueling Ajax and Achilles, Cumberland's ammunition, and Renown and Ark Royal approaching at high speed.
